newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing defense set to put on its case.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing defense set to put on its case.

text.p: Defence lawyers in the Oklahoma City bombing trial were set on Thursday to launch an assault on prosecution claims that Timothy McVeigh carefully planned and carried out the federal building bombing two years ago.

The defence will present its first witness on Thursday to counter government allegations that McVeigh was responsible for the bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, that killed 168 people.
McVeigh, 29, has pleaded not guilty, and his attorneys say authorities arrested the wrong man. If convicted, the Gulf War veteran faces the death penalty.
After the prosecution rested its case on Wednesday, chief defence attorney Stephen Jones told reporters his case would last "possibly less than two weeks."
He is expected to call far fewer witneses than the 137 the government presented in an 18-day period.
McVeigh's lawyers will zero in on shoddy practices at the FBI laboratory, whose procedures were recently criticised in a Justice Department report.
The defence has already claimed that forensic samples linking McVeigh to the crime could have been contaminated.

Jones will also try to cast doubt on witnesses who have identified McVeigh, such as the owner of the rental agency who said McVeigh was the man who rented the Ryder truck allegedly used in the bombing.
But it was unclear if he would repeat the allegations, made in a pre-trial court filing, that the bombing could have been part of an international conspiracy.

Lawyers also expect the defence to call Lea McGown, owner of the Dreamland Motel in Junction City, Kansas. She has said she saw McVeigh in a Ryder truck on Easter Sunday, three days before the bombing and a day before the government says McVeigh rented the truck.
A driver who delivered Chinese food to the motel room that the government says McVeigh rented has said McVeigh was not the person who took the food.
The prosecution put three final witnesses on the stand on Wednesday to drive home the human tragedy of the blast.

Florence Rogers, chief executive of the Federal Employees Credit Union, which was on the third floor of the Murrah building, described how seven women employees she was holding a meeting with in her office were blown away by the blast.
"When I was able to stand up, all of the girls in my office had totally disappeared, with the six floors from above us on top of them. I never saw them again," she said.
Throughout its case, the prosecution shifted from the human tragedy to dry, scientific evidence, keeping the trial moving along and sustaining interest.
"It did not bore the jury. That's the first rule of litigation," David Lane, a criminal defence attorney in Denver, said.

Witnesses including McVeigh's sister have provided a motive: McVeigh's fury over what he believed was a gross injustice in the way federal agents handled the siege at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, in 1993.
The government has painted McVeigh as a right-wing fanatic whose anger over Waco drove him to methodically plan and carry out the bombing.
Testimony from other witnesses concerned McVeigh's quest in late 1994 to find components to make the bomb. An FBI scientist said he found traces of explosives on McVeigh's clothes.
But no one placed McVeigh in Oklahoma City on the day of the bombing, and his fingerprints were not found on key evidence, gaps the defence will be able to exploit.
